This weekend's weather will be dictated by a low pressure system 
tracking from central IL this morning into the Ohio Valley on 
Sunday. This occluded system is currently being driven by a closed 
500mb low slowly drifting across the Midwest. By Sunday, an 
amplifying upper air pattern sends a deepening Canadian trough 
southward across the Great Lakes which interacts with the wave and 
causes it to stretch toward the eastern Great Lakes. As the system 
works through, expect increasing humidity and coverage of showers 
that peak tonight into Sunday before waning by Sunday evening as the 
moisture is pulled east.

The 01.00z DTX raob revealed a deep layer of dry air up to 470mb 
that has prevented much more than virga thus far as upper moisture 
continues to wrap around the low upstream. However, there is a more 
concerted push of low to mid level moisture convergence working into 
the Saginaw Valley that is bringing scattered showers early this 
morning. This area will remain favored for additional showers 
through the rest of the morning, with radar presentation indicating 
transient moderate to heavier rates at times. Areas farther south 
and east should should generally see fewer showers until better 
moisture advection begins to arrive later this afternoon.

Several waves of ascent will spread across the area this afternoon 
through tonight, then into Sunday as the interaction of the two 
waves squeezes a narrow corridor of PVA overhead. This forcing 
paired with increasing low level moisture and convergence will bring 
the highest coverage of showers and embedded storms. There will be 
an increasing threat for localized heavy rainfall as the environment 
will support efficient rainfall processes. Deep saturation and moist 
adiabatic lapse rates, warm cloud depth around 12 kft, elevated 
instability of 500 to 1000 J/kg, and PWAT near the 90th percentile 
at 1.75" all support pockets of heavy rain where showers occur. Weak 
veering flow through much of the column produces Corfidi upshear 
vectors of 15 kt or less, indicating slow storm motion and potential 
for training/backbuilding convection.

Timing and placement of convection continues to carry high 
uncertainty, but signal is emerging for a flare-up near the I-69 
corridor this afternoon. This occurs along a nearly stationary 
trough developing on the northeast side of the low, and may pose a 
threat for rainfall over 1 inch within a 1 to 3 hour window. The 
higher probability for a subtle heavy rainfall (SHARS) type event 
currently looks to target areas closer to the low center in northern 
Indiana, with support from latest hi-res QPF output. However, this 
potential may migrate northeast toward the Metro Detroit to Port 
Huron vicinity overnight into Sunday morning as the northeast 
quadrant of the system and the associated mesoscale deformation/fgen 
forcing and moisture convergence track through. With the 
shifting/stretching character of the low on Sunday, confidence 
remains low in these finer details which still may not be resolved 
well in guidance. Debated the need for a Flood Watch for the urban 
corridor which would be the most susceptible to heavy rainfall, but 
preference is to allow 12z and 18z guidance and morning trends to be 
evaluated in the decision. Latest ensemble QPF probabilities through 
Sunday remain supportive of rainfall on the order of 0.25" to 0.75" 
for much of the SE MI, with potential for 2+" in locations that see 
training convection. That being said, there is also a non-zero 
chance that certain areas receive very little rainfall given the 
scale of convection.

Drier air begins to arrive on Sunday as high pressure builds in from 
the north, but showers may continue well into the afternoon for the 
eastern forecast area before tapering off by Sunday evening. The 
high pressure takes residence overhead on Monday, promoting dry and 
seasonable conditions. The southern portion of the weekend system 
will get pinched off into a cutoff low early next week, with latest 
guidance carrying it farther south into the Tennessee Valley and 
southern Appalachians. This supports dry conditions into Tuesday as 
well. Moisture with this low eventually begins to migrate northeast, 
possibly clipping the area on Wednesday with diurnally driven 
showers. The next cold front works across the region late Thursday 
into Friday with additional chances of showers and storms.
